definition: A derivative is a financial contract whose value is derived from the value of some other asset (the underlying asset). Trading a derivative transfers only the contract and its obligations, not the underlying commodity itself — physical delivery, if any, happens only when the contract is exercised.
core_idea: Most energy trading activity is really the transfer of paper obligations about the future (futures, forwards, swaps, options) rather than the movement of physical commodities; the underlying asset is commonly a real asset like crude oil or electricity, but can also be another derivative (e.g., an option on a forward).
key_points: Common derivative types named: futures, forwards, swaps, option contracts.
The value of a derivative equals the price someone will pay to have the contract (the obligation) transferred to them.
An underlying asset can itself be a derivative — e.g., an option written on a forward contract.
relationships: Depends on the underlying asset being tradable per the assignability/liquidity/fungibility framework — formalized in accounting as 'readily convertible to cash' (RCC).
trading_implications: Because only the contract changes hands (not the commodity) until exercise, derivatives let traders take positions on price without managing physical logistics.
caveats: Trading a crude oil futures contract does not move physical crude oil at trade time — delivery only occurs upon exercise of the contract.
